basics.name: Xiangjian Zeng
basics.label: Ph.D. Student, Electrical Engineering and Computer Science
basics.summary: Ph.D. student developing closed-loop auditory stimulation to enhance cerebrospinal fluid flow during sleep. Co-author of a 2026 Science Translational Medicine paper on this work.

work.name: Lewis Lab, Massachusetts Institute of Technology
work.summary: Closed-loop auditory modulation of cerebrospinal fluid during sleep, and automatic sleep staging for simultaneous EEG-fMRI
highlights: Develop real-time EEG processing and machine-learning-based slow-oscillation phase-prediction algorithms for precisely timed closed-loop auditory stimulation during sleep
Integrate simultaneous EEG-fMRI with electrophysiological and CSF-flow measurements to quantify stimulation-evoked neural and physiological dynamics across younger and older adults
Co-authored a Science Translational Medicine paper showing that closed-loop auditory stimulation in phase with sleep slow waves enhances cerebrospinal fluid flow in humans
Benchmark automatic sleep-staging models on manually staged simultaneous EEG-fMRI and characterize systematic failures under scanner-domain shift
Investigate contributions from temporal and context priors, sensor and reference mismatch, and scanner-related signal differences

work.name: Insanally Lab, University of Pittsburgh
work.summary: Bayesian ensemble neural decoding and biologically constrained spiking recurrent neural networks
highlights: Developed a probabilistic ensemble neural decoder combining inter-spike-interval conditional probabilities across neurons to predict behavioral trial conditions

Showed that non-classically responsive neurons interact with responsive neurons during learning, and that aggregating their population activity raised behavioral decoding accuracy from 60% to 65% in late-stage learning
Built 1,000-unit spiking recurrent neural-network models in Python and Julia under biological constraints to simulate cortical dynamics underlying auditory discrimination
Investigated how flexible network dynamics emerge from balanced excitatory and inhibitory activity

work.name: Chamanzar Lab, Carnegie Mellon University
highlights: Developed an automated neural-probe waveguide characterization pipeline integrating computer vision, robotics, and signal processing
Enabled non-destructive loss measurement previously achievable primarily through destructive methods, and first-authored a peer-reviewed conference proceedings paper

work.name: Lerman Lab, UC San Diego
work.summary: Adaptive neural signal processing and peripheral nerve magnetoneurography
highlights: Developed and hardware-validated an adaptive filtering algorithm for peripheral nerve recordings, achieving approximately 45 dB suppression of 60 Hz interference; first author at the North American Neuromodulation Society meeting
Matlab signal processing for magnetic nervous system recordings; human trial test subject

highlights: Automatic cell recognition for fluorescence brain slices in Matlab with accuracy close to expert manual selection
